Hi Dirk and Mike,

Good to hear that a brand new version is due soon! Dirk, I would try installing gfortran first, to avoid having to downgrade R and re-install all packages and so on... I have been using NicheMapR this way and I have not found any bug or anything (correct me if I am wrong, Mike).

If you chose to install gfortran, first, you have to go to this link:

https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/GFortranBinaries#

Then, select your operating system, and download the appropriate file. If you are using a PC I guess that "Official MinGW builds" might be the file for you. After installing that file in your computer, re-install NicheMapR in R by using the next command:

devtools::install_github("mrke/NicheMapR")

I downloaded the gfortran build for macOS Sierra (10.12) although I am using a mac OS 10.13, and it worked.

Hope this helps.

All the best,
Urtzi

This string has been very helpful but I'm still having a similar problem to the original one described, with the output only providing values for the last location. Can either of you see where I went wrong?

graphics.off()

)

setwd("C:/Users/evelyn/Documents/My Box Files/Publications/Batrachoseps climate morphology/19Sept2018_analysis")

saldata<- read.csv("Batrac_CA_w_data_5_head_norock.csv", header=TRUE)#all spp locality data

long<-saldata$LONGITUDE#loop_plate[i,1]
lat<-saldata$LATITUDE#loop_plate[i,2]

soiltype<- saldata$soilty_num#loop_plate[i,3]
slope<- saldata$slope_combo#loop_plate[i,4]
aspect<- saldata$aspect_combo#loop_plate[i,5]
elev<- saldata$elev_combo#loop_plate[i,6]
minshade <- saldata$minshadeNZ#loop_plate[i,7]
maxshade<- saldata$maxshadeNZ#loop_plate[i,8]
BB<- saldata$BB#loop_plate[i,9]
PE<- saldata$PE#loop_plate[i,10]
KS<- saldata$KS#loop_plate[i,11]
BD<- saldata$BD#loop_plate[i,12]

L<- c(0, 0, 8.2, 8.0, 7.8, 7.4, 7.1, 6.4, 5.8, 4.8, 4.0, 1.8, 0.9, 0.6, 0.8, 0.4 ,0.4, 0, 0) * 10000 # root density at each node, mm/m3 (from Campell 1985 Soil Physics with Basic, p. 131)

                    REFL = 0.15, slope = loop_plate[i,4], aspect = loop_plate[i,5], elev = loop_plate[i,6], DEP = c(0., 2.5,  5.,  10.,  15,  20,  30,  50,  100,  200), minshade = loop_plate[i,7],
                    maxshade = loop_plate[i,8], BB = loop_plate[i,9],
                    PE = loop_plate[i,10], KS = loop_plate[i,11],
                    BD = loop_plate[i,12],Usrhyt = 0.01, L = L, LAI = LAI, runmoist = 1, snowmodel = 1)

soilmoist.out<-as.data.frame(micro$soilmoist)
shadmoist.out<-as.data.frame(micro$shadmoist)
loc.out<-as.data.frame(micro$loc)
#COLWELL_ID<-as.data.frame(saldata$COLWELL_ID)
}

write.csv(micro,"C:/Users/evelyn/Documents/My Box Files/Publications/Batrachoseps climate morphology/19Sept2018_analysis/micro_out.csv")

messages.subject: Re: Looping?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

You are experiencing that issue because, although you are running the loop for all your locations, after that, you are just saving the last micro object outside the for loop. What is exactly what you want?

If you want to save to your machine the micro objects for each location, you should insert the write.csv() function inside the for loop, and ensure that each time it saves the object you feed the write.csv function with a different name (to avoid overwritting files).

However, one is usually interested in only a few parameters estimated by NicheMapR. If that is your case, it would be better to extract those parameters (e.g. saving them into a dataframe or a list) inside the loop. As far as I can see in your code, you stored these objects: soilmoist.out and shadmoist.out, but you did not save them.

If you provide more details about how you want the for loop to behave, I will be able to give you a more precise answer.

All the best,
Urtzi

messages.subject: Re: Looping?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thank you for specifying your goal!

After running NicheMapR with your parameters, you get 1440 soil moisture values (24h * 12 days * 5 years) per shading level and location. Thus, I am assuming that you want all those profiles to be saved (i.e. all those dataframes). The only solution that comes into my mind is to create a list, store all the dataframes for each location in a list inside the big lists, and finally save the big list as an RData file. You can always load your results back into R.

Here you have the code that does this (I haven't changed anything in the first lines of your code):

ls.moist <- list() # you create an empty list

for (i in 1:nrow(loop_plate)){
  micro<-micro_global(loc = c(loop_plate[i,1], loop_plate[i,2]), timeinterval = 12, nyears = 5, soiltype = loop_plate[i,3],
                      REFL = 0.15, slope = loop_plate[i,4], aspect = loop_plate[i,5], elev = loop_plate[i,6], DEP = c(0., 2.5,  5.,  10.,  15,  20,  30,  50,  100,  200), minshade = loop_plate[i,7],
                      maxshade = loop_plate[i,8], BB = loop_plate[i,9],
                      PE = loop_plate[i,10], KS = loop_plate[i,11],
                      BD = loop_plate[i,12],Usrhyt = 0.01, L = L, LAI = LAI, runmoist = 1, snowmodel = 1)

  soilmoist.out<-as.data.frame(micro$soilmoist)
  shadmoist.out<-as.data.frame(micro$shadmoist)

  loc.out<-as.data.frame(micro$longlat) # Changed loc to longlat. I am guessing that that's what you want.

  ls.moist[[i]] <- list(loc=loc.out, solmoist=soilmoist.out, shadmoist=shadmoist.out) # create a named list an store inside the big list (ls.moist)
}

str(ls.moist, max.level=2) # you can see that ls.moist is a list of 4 (each location). For each location you have a list of three (with loc, solmoist, and shadmoist)

save(ls.moist, file='moisture_list.RData') # you can save this as an RData file

rm(list=ls()) # then remove everything
load('./moisture_list.RData') # and re-load results

If you see the way to get all those results in a csv (or if you are aiming for soil moisture at an specific depth), just let me know and I will try to change the code!

All the best! ~u

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

That is very likely. If I am not wrong, you are using the environmental layers that come with the NicheMapR installation (i.e. New et al. 2002 data), right? That is what micro_global() does when you don't use other environmental data as input. Then, you can load that dataset with these commands:

# just to find the folder where you downloaded global_climate.nc <http://global_climate.nc>. Alternatively, if you know the path, just use it
gcfolder <- paste(.libPaths()[1], "/gcfolder.rda", sep = "")
load(gcfolder)

# load the dataset
global_climate <- raster::brick(paste(folder, "/global_climate.nc <http://global_climate.nc>", sep = ""))
plot(global_climate[[1]]) # first layer

You can crop those layers (or just the first one) to your study area, and look if they fall outside mainland.

Good luck with that!

All the best, ~u

All the best,
